title: Tax Structures in Developing Countries: Many Puzzles and a Possible Explanation
research_question: Why do tax structures in developing countries differ so systematically from those in developed countries — featuring lower revenue/GDP, minor reliance on personal labor income taxes, heavy reliance on corporate income taxes, tariffs, and seignorage, large informal sectors, and dramatic variation in effective tax rates across firms? What single underlying friction can rationalize this constellation of policy choices, and what does it imply for the role of inflation, trade protection, restrictions on foreign firms and banks, state ownership of banks, and bureaucratic red tape?
data_description: The paper draws on cross-country macro-fiscal data covering the years 1996–2001, with the country as the unit of observation. Sources include the IMF's Government Finance Statistics Yearbook and International Finance Statistics Yearbook, and the World Bank's World Development Indicators. Key variables include GDP per capita, total tax revenue as a share of GDP, the composition of revenue (personal income taxes, corporate income taxes, consumption/production taxes, trade/border taxes, seignorage), inflation rates, and estimates of the size of the informal economy as a share of GDP (from Schneider 2002, using a currency-demand approach, for 1999). The authors also assemble maximum statutory tax rates (corporate, personal, VAT) for 26 developing and 19 developed countries from worldwide-tax.com. Countries are grouped by World Bank income categories (low, lower-middle, middle, high), and weighted averages are computed within each group.
institutional_context: The setting is the contrast between fiscal systems in low- and middle-income economies and those in advanced economies. Poorer countries collect about two-thirds the revenue/GDP of richer ones, lean heavily on corporate taxes, tariffs, and seignorage, make limited use of personal income taxation, and host very large informal/cash sectors (a median of 37% of GDP, ranging from 13% in Hong Kong/Singapore to 76% in Nigeria), while OECD informal sectors average around 15%. Effective tax rates vary enormously across firms within a country: capital-intensive enterprises dependent on banks face high liabilities, while many firms operate entirely in cash and escape taxation. These economies are also characterized by frequent state ownership of banks, capital controls, restrictions on foreign bank entry, tariff protection of capital-intensive industries, higher inflation, and pervasive red tape — institutional features that motivate the inquiry into how limited financial-sector development shapes feasible tax policy.
